title: Boss: it worked on my laptop
summary: Three scripts written on Windows fail on the Linux build agents. Read the errors, find the cause, fix them so they run anywhere.

steps.title: Ticket BUILD-871
body: *"We moved the nightly jobs from my laptop to the Linux agents (PowerShell 7.6). Three of them broke. The scripts did
not change, so it must be the agents."*
It is not the agents. Each script relies on something that only happened to be true on one machine: an alias, the
current folder, the console. Run each one, read the first line of the error (or the wrong output), fix it.

steps.title: ls: invalid option
prompt: Run `pwsh -File ~/scripts/newest-logs.ps1`. It should print the names of the **three most recently changed `.log`
files** under `~/logs`, newest last. Make it work here (and still on Windows): every command and parameter spelt out.

checks.name: prints the three newest logs, newest last
checks.fail: It should print `a.log`, `app.log` and `d.log`, one per line. Compare with `Get-ChildItem ~/logs -Recurse -Filter *.log | Sort-Object LastWriteTime | Select-Object Name, LastWriteTime`.

checks.name: no aliases left
checks.cmd: pwsh -NoProfile -c 'Invoke-ScriptAnalyzer -Path ~/scripts/newest-logs.ps1 -IncludeRule PSAvoidUsingCmdletAliases | ForEach-Object Message'; grep -Eq '(^|[|] *)(ls|sort|select|%) ' ~/scripts/newest-logs.ps1 && echo 'short names still in the script'
checks.fail: Spell out every command: `Get-ChildItem`, `Sort-Object`, `Select-Object`, `ForEach-Object`. (`ls` and `sort` are not even aliases on Linux, so the analyzer cannot see them.)

hints: The error comes from `/usr/bin/ls`, the GNU program: on Linux, `ls` is not an alias of `Get-ChildItem`.
`sort` is the same story: `Get-Command sort` shows `/usr/bin/sort`.
solution: Set-Content ~/scripts/newest-logs.ps1 -Value '# newest-logs.ps1: the three most recently changed logs, newest last.', 'Get-ChildItem ~/logs -Recurse -Filter *.log | Sort-Object LastWriteTime | Select-Object -Last 3 | ForEach-Object { $_.Name }'
steps.explain: `Get-Command <name> -All` shows every command a name could mean and which one wins. When a script has to run on Linux agents too, test it there in CI (a `pwsh` job on an Ubuntu runner costs nothing) rather than finding out from the nightly run.

steps.title: The term 'Get-Greeting' is not recognized
prompt: The scheduler starts jobs **from `/`**. Reproduce it: `Set-Location /; pwsh -File ~/scripts/nightly.ps1`. Read both errors.
Fix `~/scripts/nightly.ps1` so it works from **any** current folder and prints

checks.name: works when started from /
checks.expectOutput: Good night, platform. Backups start at 01:00.
checks.fail: Started from `/`, the script should print only the greeting.

checks.name: works when started from /tmp
checks.expectOutput: Good night, platform. Backups start at 01:00.
checks.fail: Started from `/tmp`, the script should print only the greeting.

hints: First error: `./lib.ps1` means *the current folder*, which is `/` under the scheduler, not the script's folder. `$PSScriptRoot` is the folder the running script is in.
Second error: `& script.ps1` runs it in a **child scope**, so the functions it defines are gone when it returns. Dot-sourcing (`. script.ps1`) runs it in the caller's scope.
explain: Two habits for every script: build paths from `$PSScriptRoot` (`Join-Path $PSScriptRoot 'config.json'`), never from
the current folder; and load helper files with `.` (or better, make them a module and `Import-Module` it: module 5).
`&` is for *running* something; `.` is for *loading* it into your scope.

steps.title: Found 0 stale files
prompt: `pwsh -File ~/scripts/stale.ps1` prints three paths and then `Found 0 stale files`, so the clean-up job that runs after
it never deletes anything. Run it with its output captured to see the problem: `$out = pwsh -File ~/scripts/stale.ps1`,
Fix `Get-StaleFile` so it **returns** the stale files instead of only showing them. The last line must become

checks.name: Found 3 stale files
checks.fail: The last line should be `Found 3 stale files`.

checks.name: the function returns objects, not screen text
checks.fail: `Write-Host` writes to the screen (the host), not to the pipeline. Output the file object (or `Write-Output $file`) instead.

hints: `$out` shows only `Found 0 stale files`: the three paths never reached the pipeline, they went straight to the console.
In PowerShell a function returns **everything it outputs**, not just what follows `return`. A bare `$file` on its own line outputs it.
explain: `Write-Host` is for messages a human reads (and in PowerShell 5+ it goes to the *information* stream, number 6, so
`6>$null` hides it). Data goes to the *success* stream: just output it. Every value a function does not capture or
send to `$null` becomes part of its return value, which is also why stray output like a `.Add()` call's return
value can sneak into results: `[void]$list.Add($x)` or `$null = ...` silences it.
